Church Government
CHURCH GUHV-ern-muhnt
n. (a doctrine of ecclesiology; church polity)
From church, Old English cirice from Greek kyriakon, belonging to the Lord, and government, from Latin gubernare, to steer or rule. The term names the manner in which Christ orders and rules His Church.

📖 Biblical Definition

Church government is the biblical ordering of Christ’s Church for her worship, discipline, and edification, established not by human preference but by the appointment of her sovereign Head. The New Testament reveals Christ ruling His Church by His Word and Spirit through officers He has instituted. Scripture names two ordinary and perpetual offices: the elder, also called overseer or pastor, charged with teaching, ruling, and shepherding the flock; and the deacon, charged with the ministry of mercy and the care of the church’s practical affairs. The qualifications for both are laid down in the apostolic letters, and the offices are reserved, in keeping with the complementarian order God has set, to men called and gifted of God. The Scriptures further show a plurality of elders in each congregation, for the apostles ordained elders, in the plural, in every church, that no single man should lord it over Christ’s heritage but that the flock be shepherded by a council of qualified men under Christ. With this stands the congregation’s own responsibility: the gathered church is called to receive sound teaching, to exercise discipline, to guard the purity of her membership, and to honor and submit to her lawful officers in the Lord. The 1689 Confession sets forth this pattern: Christ alone is Head and Lawgiver of His Church, no man may add offices or laws He has not appointed, and the regulative principle that governs worship governs polity as well. Church government rightly ordered guards the gospel, feeds the sheep, and keeps the Church in subjection to her one true King.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The biblical ordering of Christ’s Church through the two offices of elder and deacon, a plurality of elders, and congregational responsibility under Christ the Head.

CHURCH GOVERNMENT, n. From church, Greek kyriakon, the Lord’s, and government, Latin gubernare, to rule; the manner in which Christ orders His Church.

The ordering of the Church for worship, discipline, and edification by Christ’s own appointment.

Comprising two perpetual offices: elder (overseer, pastor) and deacon.

Marked by a plurality of qualified men as elders and the responsibility of the gathered congregation.

Founded on the apostolic practice: “And when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Acts 14:23).

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

1 Tim 3:1 — "This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work."

Tit 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

1 Pet 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Biblical polity is corrupted on one side by hierarchies Christ never appointed and on the other by disorder that despises the offices He did appoint.

expand to see more

One corruption multiplies offices and powers Scripture nowhere grants—the ascending ranks of prelacy and, supremely, the papal monarchy, which exalts one man as universal head over the whole Church. But Christ alone is Head of the Church (Ephesians 1:22), and Peter, far from claiming dominion, charged the elders to feed the flock not as lords but as examples (1 Peter 5:2–3). To add offices and rulers Christ has not appointed is to usurp His crown rights and to bind consciences with the commandments of men. The remedy is the plain New Testament pattern of elders and deacons, with no rank above the local eldership but Christ Himself.

An opposite corruption is the disorder that despises office altogether, whether the egalitarian rejection of the male eldership God has appointed or a rugged individualism that submits to no shepherd. Yet the apostles ordained elders in every church (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5) and reserved the office to qualified men, and believers are commanded to obey those who have the rule over them and to submit. To recover biblical church government is to walk between hierarchy and chaos, honoring the offices Christ instituted, the plurality of elders He ordained, and the congregation’s responsibility under His sole headship.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Biblical polity roots in Christ’s sole headship and His appointment of elders and deacons over His Church.

expand to see more

Christ alone is Head and Lawgiver of His Church.

Two perpetual offices are appointed: elder and deacon.

Each congregation is shepherded by a plurality of qualified male elders.

The gathered congregation bears responsibility for discipline and purity.

The 1689 Confession sets forth this New Testament pattern of polity.

Usage

"“Sound church government guards the gospel and feeds the flock.”"

"“The apostles ordained a plurality of elders in every church.”"

"“Biblical church government knows no head above the local eldership but Christ.”"
